Simply because the sentiment behind the Act in the province of Quebec was different from the sentiment behind the Act in the other provinces. What are the underlying causes of the disturbances which have taken place in Quebec city and in other parts

of the province of Quebec? About eight years ago, speaking in this House, I made the statement that there was in the province of Quebec an antiBritish or anti-imperial sentiment. I was severely taken to task by hon. members on both sides of the House for having so expressed myself, but within the last few years, since the war started, the conduct of the province of Queibec has thoroughly justified my statement of seven or eight years ago. If there is such a sentiment in the province of Quebec, why does it exist? I believe that it does exist, although I am sorry to hold that belief. I think the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Maokie) struck the nail squarely on the head this evening in the excellent speech he made when he said that in that province they have different ideals, and that there has'been wrong teaching. Wrong teaching by whom? Mr. Speaker, I do not want to go into details, or to go back into the history of this country, but were I so disposed I could quote different utterances of the leader of the Opposition which, in imy judgment, have not been conducive to cementing the relations between Queibec and the other provinces of the Dominion and the Mother Country. I could, if I so desired, quote many utterances of the right hon. gentleman which have furnished an excuse to those in the province of Queibec who desire an excuse for evading military service. I have them under my hand; I could give them to the House; I have done so on more occasions than one. Moreover, I have done so in the presence of the right horn, leader of the Opposition; so that I cannot be accused of saying in his absence what I would not say in his presence. I regret it as much as any man who wishes to see this country what I believe it was intended to be, a great country, and what it can only be if we have a united people. Those of the province of Queibec who have enlisted and gone to the front have proved themselves as courageous and as 'brave as any men who have left the shores of Canada; I have that from personal conversation with different officers who have stood with these men over there, and. I cannot think that these men who have gone overseas and helped to make the record that Canada has achieved are different from the great majority of the people of the province of Quebec; but there are certain elements in the province of Quebec which have kept those people from doing their duty, and I propose to state in just a few words what those elements are.
First of all, I say that one of the causes for the sentiment which exists in that prov-

inee-and this is hack of the rioting which has taken place there recently, and back of the hostility to the Military Service Act,- is men like Bourassa and Lavergne who have misled the people of that province, and inasmuch as Bourassa and Lavergne repeat in their speeches statements which have fallen from the lips of the right hon. leader of the Opposition I hold him primarily responsible as the original teacher of those false doctrines, and he must bear his share of the responsibility. There is a way of dealing with men like Bourassa and Lavergne-a way which I suggested in this House a couple of years ago, on more than one occasion. Lavergne should have been stripped of his rank as colonel long ago, because he is a disgrace to the rank he holds; that also should have been done out of regard to the men who were in khaki and are in khaki at the present time. It is all nonsense to say that if you do that, you will place him on a pedestal as a martyr, which' is just what he wants. I do not believe it for a moment. You put a man like Lavergne or Bourassa behind the bars for treasonable or seditious utterance, and do you think he will boast of the fact that he is behind the bars? Not on your life. He will whine like the cur he is. That is one way of dealing with that sort of people.
Another thing that should be done is to suppress, and suppress immediately, papers like Le Devoir which have not scrupled to scatter their seditious doctrines throughout Quebec and so influence the minds of the people. We are in a state of war and these matters should not be handled with kid gloves. It is either right for a paper to be allowed to circulate that publishes seditious language, or it is wrong, and I do not think there is a man in this House who thinks it is right that such a paper should circulate, and it seems to me,, then that the only thing we have to ask ourselves is: Has this paper circulated seditious utterances, and does it continue to do so? If so, our course of action is clear; there is only one thing to do.
There is another cause for all the trouble in Quebec, and I will refer toi it in just a word. I have said that I believe that one of the causes of the trouble is wrong teaching by such men as I have referred to. Another cause for this wrong attitude and mistaken sentiment on the part of the majority of the people in the province of Quebec is the attitude of the Roman Catholic church in that province. For some reason or other, the attitude of the great majority of the Roman Catholic clergy of that province is opposed to the Military Service Act, and opposed to this country taking its part in the war which we in Ontario and other provinces think it should take. 1 have never in my life uttered one word derogatory of the religion of -any -man,, and I hope I never shall. It is not my purpose to discuss the .rights and wrongs of this or that religious belief. I wi-^h every man, no matter what his religious belief may be, Godspeed on his journey as he sees it through lif-e, and I hope he will succeed in getting to -the proper place when he leaves this world. But while I h-ave no word of. criticism in regard to the Roman Catholic religion, I -say that when -a church, be it Roman (Catholic, Presbyterian or any other denomination, enters -the domain of politics and takes -an active -and influencing part in directing the -destinies of this country, and tells the people what to do in a great crisis such a-s this, I have a perfect right to discuss the matter with them. II do not attack their right to express their views; lif they wish to enter the arena and place th-ei-r reasons before the public they have a perfect right to do so; but I trust th-at no person will then find fault with me if -I pass my opinion upon -their views.
I do not intend to state here why the attitude of -the Roman Ca-tholi-c church in the province of. Quebec is what I believe it t-o be, but I d-o- say that in those two reasons- the hostility of the majority of the clergy of that province to the Military Service Act and to full participation by Canada in the war, and -secondly, to. wrong teaching by such -men a-s I have alluded to-you have the -causes leading up to- the -disturbances which took place in- the city of Quebec last week.

Mr. Speaker, when I was elected to represent in this House of Commons of Canada the constituency of Dorchester, I was under the impression that I would be called here to give, according to the very modest experience which I possess, my views on the legislation which would be submitted for consideration. I have been here now ten days, and I have listened very attentively to the discussions which have taken place. I have had two surprises already, and perhaps I shall have more before the session is ended, Last year, the whole press of this country, Liberal and Tory, proclaimed to the country that a Union Government had been formed, composed of the best elements of our population, to help Canada take her part in the war. But since the session

commenced, we have seen just what kind of Union Government it was that, 'was formed at Ottawa. Last week my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce introduced a Bill, and hon. members on his own side of the House took occasion to make a very violent attack on the minister.
On the Bill.

The minister was behind the Bill, or the Bill was in front of the minister. I think the minister was more badly hit than the Bill because the Bill passed. When I left Quebec a day or so ago, I * looked into the faces of women who had lived hours of tragedy and of drama. We had soldiers in our streets of Quebec by the thousands. Every street corner wais guarded with machine iguns. Quebec was practically under martial law. We were experiencing all the difficulties and troubles of actual war. Nevertheless hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House take the occasion of these troubles to bring on a debate, and not to remedy the conditions, not to suggest measures which would bring peace to the people in Quebec and throughout the rest of [DOT]the Dominion. When the hon. member for North Simeoe (Mr. Currie) rose in this House, he rose, not as a patriot, not as a Canadian, thinking only of Canada, but he was thinking of his own petty and mean interests as a local provincial and parochial politician from Ontario.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman should qualify his language. He should withdraw the words "mean," "politician." They 'are hardly parliamentary.

I bow to your decision. 1 withdraw the words which are not parliamentary. I only wanted to point out to the House that I thought is was very unfortunate that an event of the importance and of the gravity of that which happened in Quebec should be taken as the occasion of such a debate as we have heard in the House to-day. Have we spoken, Mr. Speaker, of the riots in Quebec? Have the members on the other side of the House suggested remedies? I was sorry to hear the hon. member for Fronteruac (Mr. Edwards) making an attack on the Roman Catholic clergy. I have heard members on the other side making attacks on the right hon. leader of the Opposition. I have heard them making attacks on the French Canadians as a race. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry. I thought in this House of 'Commons of Canada that, no mat-

ter what province you came from, no matter what nationality you belonged to, no matter what creed you believed in, there was one ideal which was common to everybody-the love of our common country. I do not think, Sir, that discussions like that which took place to-day will help Canada to become the big, prosperous and great nation she should become. Hon. members on the other side of the House have been very wide in their remarks. The scope of* their speeches has extended over the whole political situation in Canada. They have pointed out different reasons for the situation which exists in Quebec to-day. Will you let me say that the members of the Government are responsible for the situation in Quebec to-day, on account of the policy which they have followed, on account of the policy which they persist in, unfortunately, to-day, of coercing the province.
I do not wish to say that the ministers have bad intentions; I do not wish to say the Government is doing it with the object of arousing ill-feeling in the province of Quebec. But I say that the attitude of the Government for the last four or-five years has been of such a nature that ill-feeling has been aroused, and that the Government ought to take measures to appease the people of Quebec. What happened, Mr. Speaker? We have heard the member for North Simeoe (Mr. Currie), the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) talking about Mr. Bourassa, talking about Mr. Armand Lavergne and saying that Bourassa and Armand Lavergne were the real cause of the whole trouble. I .am not here to defend Bourassa. I have never been a political supporter of Mr. Bourassa, and never endorsed his political ideas. On the contrary, I have .always fought his candidates. I was a candidate in 1911 in the county of Charlevoix. I stood there as a Liberal candidate, supporting the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I stood for the Naval Bill introduced by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and I stood for participation by Canada in Imperial wars. But at that time Mr. Bourassa was not denounced by the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), nor by the member for North Simeoe (Mr. Currie), as a cause of danger or as a reason for sedition in the province of Quebec. Bourassa was brought by the friends of the hon. members in the province of Ontario, and he spoke to the people of Ontario in order to defeat the hon. leader of the Opposition. What was the programme of Mr. Bourassa at that time? I do not wish to insist on

this point., but I only want to point out that in 1911 Bourassa and his school, supported, financed, paid' and organized by the Tory party, went through the province of Quebec, and said that we did not owe anything to England, and they were applauded by members of the Tory party who -afterwards became members of the Borden Government. Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind the House of one incident. In the byelection in 1910, in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, I supported the policy of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who was leading the fight against the Conservative candidate. Mr. Monk was a minister in the Borden Cabinet. Mr. Sevigny, Mr. Blondin and Mr. Lavergne were there. And who was supplying the money to beat the Liberal candidate? The Montreal organization, backed and inspired by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), if my information is reliable. That night, when the result of the election in Drummond-Arthabaska was announced- the hon. Minister of Railways laughs. He may laugh, but I am quite convinced he knows what I am saying now is true.
An ihon. MEMBER: You have got the wrong minister.

On election night, when the Liberal candidate was defeated, when the Nationalist doctrine in Quebec received its first support and triumph, a member of the present Government telegraphed Ar-mand Lavergne and said: "Anything to beat Laurier." The hon. member for North Simcoe, this afternoon rose in this House to inquire about the reason of the riots in Quebec. I will give the real reasons. I have given the first, and I will give later the proximate reason of these riots. Let us go further, and examine the history of the last five years. When the elections of 1911 were held in Ontario,the Tory organization, led by the then Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), waved the British flag, and said that in the province of Quebec everybody was disloyal and everybody was a traitor, whereas in the same province, Armand Lavergne, Henri Bourassa and all that crowd were fighting the fight of the Tory party.
You succeeded1. The Tory party came into power. Those who had promised in the counties of Ontario, and ini the counties of the English provinces, to save the British Empire, were the first to give the fattest portfolios to their new Nationalist friends to reward them for their share in the victory. Canada had thiis extraordinary and
remarkable spectacle of an ultra loyalist like the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) sitting close: to Mr. Monk, who would not fight for England. That is the second causie of the riots in Quebec. It was the want of sincerity on the part of our public men when the Cabinet was formed.
Let us go farther. A gentleman who is still a member of the Cabinet, although he is not a member of this House or a member of the Senate, a man who is kept in this Cabinet against every principle'of constitutional law, a man who has no right to sit in the Cabinet because he has no responsibility towards the people, a man who bored holes in the British flag in many counties in Quebec, has been drawing ?7,000 from the Crown since my right hon. friend has been the Prime Minister of this country. Third reason for the riots in Quebec.
My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) wants to know why the people of Quebec are displeased. I will tell him. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that a province IiKe the province of Quebec, which has been the pioneer province of this country, a province that has sent to this Parliament the brightest men that Canadian politics had known, will consent to be represented by a mian who has lost his deposit in one constituency and who lias been beaten in another 'by 2,000 votes? French Canadians may have defects, tout they have one quality, and that is the quality of self-respect. When a race has self-respect that race has the right to be respected by the Government of the country. Fourth reason for the riots in Quebec.
My hon. friend from Frontenae (Mr. Edwards) claims that Le Devoir ought to be suppressed. I am also of that opinion. Suppress it. But I am sure of one thing, and that is that the Government has not the courage to do it. It is no use coming . before this House to lie to the country. What we want are the facts and nothing else. Le Devoir is a menace; suppress it. Orders in Council are easily passed. Why will not Le Devoir be suppressed? I will tell you-because it is financed by Tory money. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) is the man who financed Le Devoir in 1911 so as to beat my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for St. Antoine isi not in the House. I am sorry. If he were here I would say just the same thing.
And he would not deny it.

The money that was
given to Le Devoir to preach this doctrine of sedition, this unpatriotic principle of nonparticipation 'by Canada in Imperial wars, came from the Tory party. Every word which was- printed, every eheet that was distributed in Quebec was paid for with Tory money-
An hon. MEM-BEE: The country's money.

And probably the country's money. How is that money being reimbursed to the hon. member for St. Antoine?-boot contracts for the troops over in Europe. Mr. Speaker, that is the fifth reason for the riots in Quebec.
I wish to congratulate my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) on the very moderate speech which he has made. I have had very bad information about the hon. member. I understand that last year there was a certain discussion into which my humble personality was mixed and certain things that were said were reported to me. I am quite sure that my hon. friend from Simcoe was not in as good humour then as he was to-day. I congratulate him and I also congratulate the hon. the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes). I can tell my hon. friend that in Quebec there are some people who do not like him. Why, I do not know. If my hon. friend would go to Quebec oftener and speak the way he has spoken to-night everybody'would like him. -The unfortunate side of the situation between Ontario and Quebec is that the people of Ontario do not travel often enough in Quefbec. If the tw-o peoples w-ould meet, if the two populations would mix, all this friction would soon disappear and this trouble would be a thing of -the past.
I am quite sure, Sir, that you have heard it said in the House that I was a rebel. It has been said. It was said, I understand, last year that if I was elected to this House, I would not be allowed to take my seat because I was worse than Louis Riel.
Who said that?

I forget who said it. I
am very charitable and even if I did remember who said it I would pretend that I did not remember. But I can tell this House that I am no rebel, that I am a plain, simple, good-intentioned Liberal.
Because we are here.

It may be that the hon. gentleman does not know, but I do know. Why are we here? To pass Daylight Saving Bills? To be consulted on petty and mean measures? To deal with what the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) the other day called fads and freaks? But when it is proposed to suspend the common law of our country, ta close the courts of our provinces, to deprive the population of liberty and freedom and constitutional privileges, we, the representatives of the people, are not consulted. Mr. Speaker, your parliamentary experience is very wide, but I should be surprised if you could quote a precedent from British, Canadian or American constitutional history-I shall not say similar, but even a slightly analogous instance-to justify the step which the Prime Minister of Canada has taken to-day. Motions are called, and without giving us the right to discuss the matter the Prime Minister lays on the Table an Order in Council destroying every constitutional guarantee that we in the province of Quebec and you in the other provinces have. Is that fair? Is that the proper way to govern this country? I say that it is not. What are the aims and objects of the allied nations in the great war which is now being fought? It is that of maintaining liberty and freedom for the universe and for humanity.
An hon. MIEMIBER:	Hear, hear.

I hear an hon. gentleman .say " hear, hear." I believe it is an hon. gentleman who has fought for liberty and freedom in Flanders, and I congratulate him on having done so. I would ask him, however, to put the same energy into fighting in this country for the preservation and maintenance of the freedom of his own people. The House of Commons of Canada has today witnessed as sad a spectacle as ever w.as witnessed by any Parliament in the British Empire. Why so? Because, first, this Order in Council has destroyed every constitutional guarantee; and, second, in this country there should be no question of coercion. We should be united. Why is it that in the city of Ottawa, at the Chateau Laurier, on the street, when members of the House of Commons meet, they

exchange a friendly handshake and friend-' ly views, but the moment they enter the House they -seem to forget their friendliness and their common united interests? No matter what may have been said, the province of Quebec is very useful to the rest of the Dominion and has done much to build iup our country. Quebec has produced great statesmen; I have only to point to my right hon. leader, (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who is certainly the most distinguished man that Canadian politics has produced. The (people of Quebec want to live 'in peace with the other provinces, hut how can we live in peace unless the attitude maintained at present by certain elements of the population ceases? The Solicitor General in the present Government (Mr. Guthrie), for instance, addressing a public meeting in the province of Ontario, narrows his mind to such an extent as to declare that, luckily for Australia, it has no province of Quebec. How can you have union in this country, how can you have harmony in this country when the president of the Council makes such declarations as he did during the last election campaign? How can you have union and concord in this country when a man like the Hon. G. H. Ferguson declares on the floor of the Ontario Legislature that French Canadians are no more needed in the province of Ontario than Germans or Austrians? How can you have union in this country when you have -the press of this country insulting Quebec every day? The Orange Sentinel is a sheet whicli ought to be suppressed. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has declared that Le Devoir ought to be suppressed. I agree with him, but he ought also to agree with me in asking for the suppression of the Orange Sentinel for the same reason. Much to my surprise and astonishment the Prime Minister of this country announced this afternoon that there was a revolution and sedition in Quebec. For a definition of sedition, Mr. Speaker, I would refer you to Article 132 of the Criminal Code, and the decision given by Lord Haisbury in England. If the Prime Minister is sincere in his desire for union and peace among the peoples of this country, let him suppress the Orange Sentinel and have its editor arrested, just as Le Devoir ought to be suppressed -and its editor arrested. What is bad in Quebec is no better in Ontario. Let us hope that better days are coming. Let us hope that in the English provinces there will arise a man of the broadninded-ness of the former leaders of the parties in [Mb Cannon.]
this country. Let us 

hope that Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Oliver Mowat will have worthy successors. Let us hope that once	more from	Ontario Liberalismwill	be heard.	Let us hope thatonce	more from	Ontario a voicewill	speak as	the old Liberalsused	to speak in this Canada of
ours when- we used to fight for liberty and freedom. Let us hope the spirit of Lyou Mackenzie, of Mo-wat, Blake, Bose and Macdonald is- not dead. Let us hope that Ontario will again do something for liberal i'in in 'Canada. When we have real liberal-minded people in the English-speaking provinces, if they iwill come to our province, they will be welcomed, because in the province of Quebec there is no narrowmindedness; we are broadminded. We have sent to- this House fifteen English-speaking members elected- by fifteen French-speaking constituencies; I -should like to know w-hat county in Ontario, with an English-speaking population, would elect a French-speaking candidate. What is the use of wasting out time as we have been doing this afternoon talking about Quebec and Ontario-. There should not be any Quebec or Ontario-; it should be Canada. So- far as I am concerned, in my personal business, I do not ask whether 'a man comes from Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan, whether he is Irish, Scotch or English; as long as he lie an honest respectable Canadian, that is good enough for me. I regret that we in this country have nevieT well understood Cana-dianism. Yiou may love England. England is the mother country of the vast majority of the people of this country, and it is only natural that English-speaking people should love England. England is^ovable on acount of its- great institutions -and its great history. But why did our -forefathers come to this country? They oa-me to settle in a new country, where we could be loyal British subjects in being loyal Canadians, and I think that the moment that the people of this- country realize this truth all these small, petty, mean provincial troubles will disappear.

I have- no desire at this time of the morning to take up the time of the House, but I believe this- is- a -subject- which interests people in Canada at this time more than any other. The people of Canada are anxious to know the reason for the recent disturbances in thei city of Quebec, and I have listened with a -great deal of attention and interest to the reasons put forth by the speakers -on the o-the-r side of the House. The

last speaker, the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) asked a very pertinent question towards the dose of his remarks. He asked why we were here. He did not give an answer but I will give one. The majority of the members of this House are here to see that our men overseas get proper reinforcements, to see that eveTy part of Canada, so far as we can make laws to accomplish that purpose, shall provide an equal and fair proportion of those reinforcements. A great many reasons or excuses have been given to-day for the disturbance in Quebec. The reason put forth by the leader of the Opposition was that a certain officer employed by the Department of Justice asked a young man in a very uncivil manner to show his exemption papers, and when he could not do so, arrested him. Cbnse-quently, there was a riot, which I believe cost the lives of many innocent citizens. For the benefit of those members who do not understand the circumstances in other provinces, I may say we have exactly the same thing to contend with in Ontario and every other part of Canada. I know one point within a short distance of where I [DOT] reside where a man may be called upon to show his papers ten times a day. If he boards a train, he has to show them, most assuredly, and show them again before he gets off, and if it is a junction point he may have to show them five or six times in one afternoon; but there are no riots up there; we have killed nobody; we have not had to dig 'any one out of the snow. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who was on the ground at the time, gave a variety of reasons for the disturbances and incidentally I suppose rehearsed some of his election speech. He! said the reason the Military Service Act was enforced upon this country was in order to get rid of the poor habitant of Quebec, send him over to France and get rid of him as soon as possible. If that were our object, we have not been very successful.	A few minutes later the hon.
gentleman said that there were twenty-five to fifty thousand men on the fields of Picardy to-day from the province of Quebec. I venture to say, and I believe I can! say it without danger of successful contradiction, that there has never been in any part of France, 5,000 French Canadians at any one time. It is all right enough to' praise the 22nd Battalion, and we do it. We give the French Canadian soldier every credit, and he deserves it, but unfortunately the only infrantry battalion from Quebec which
has ever seen France is the 22nd, or about 1,000 men, We know these facts. And as a matter of fact hundreds of men were taken from Alberta and other provinces to reinforce that one single battalion, which is at the front at the present time, and these men were not even French Canadian by origin, but men speaking the English language. The hon. gentleman goes on to tell us that this Act is applied differently-or he infers that this Act is applied differently-in the province of Quebec, and that is the real cause for the riots. He does not say for an instant, that he, as .a member of this House, did anything to stop the riots-, or counsel these men in a. better way, or to lead them in the right way. We have every reason to suppose from his own words that he did nothing to counteract the trouble in Quebec.
Then we come to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). He has a different version, although he says he was present at the time, and he goes very far afield when giving the reasons for the riot in Quebec. But he went into the matter very carefully and he gave the reasons, first, second, third and fourth, and what do you suppose were the reasons which he gave? 1st he says that there was an election in the county of Drummond-Arthabaska, .and that the Grit representative was not elected That is reason number one-a Liberal candidate in the Drummond-Arthabaska election in 1910 was defeated. Reason number two is that during the election of 1911, only seven years ago, there was an unholy alliance between the Tories of that time, or some of them, and the Nationalists of Quebec. I do not intend .to take the time of this House with the discussion of a matter of this kind. We .all know it is absolutely beside the question of the present time, and it is only done for the purpose of camouflaging the real issue as it stands to-day. Reason number three was that the present Postmaster General ihad been or was drawing a salary of $7,000, and he is not' at the present time a member of the House, having been defeated in 1911.
The fourth reason was that Le Devoir had not been suppressed. I think it is idle even to discuss matters of this kind. This gentleman knows perfectly well that the only reason which can be given which will hold good in the matter of the disturbances in the province of Quebec is that these poor misguided men have been deliberately misled by the leaders in the province in which they reside. We know perfectly well that these men of themselves are peaceful, law-

abiding citizens, but they have been badly led from time to time, and they have been persuaded that if they would raise certain disturbances, or take certain action, this Government would (be weak enough, or supine enough, to allow them to get off, and permit the Act to fall into disuse.
That is absolutely false.
The hon. gentleman says that is absolutely untrue.
I do.

In the riding which I had the honour to represent in the last election this argument was used openly from the platform in places where there were French Canadian voters. It was represented to the voters that if they voted for the candidate supported by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the leader of the Opposition, he would secure for them immunity so far as military service is concerned, and personally I have not the slightest doubt that was done in every constituency in Canada where it was necessary to get the French Canadian vote.

Who was the French
Canadian leader who stated that- in the hon. gentleman's riding?

I am not talking about French Canadian leaders, but I refer to the man who opposed me, and his statements were on a parity with the statements of all the French Canadian leaders, and I know the statement was made throughout Ontario.
The hon. gentleman said Quebec just now.
I believe it was made in Quebec in exactly the same way.
It was not.

Another complaint made by the hon. gentleman from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) was that this Government had got in, and this Act was being enforced- why? Because the late Government had deprived certain citizens of the country of the right to vote; or in other words, that had we given a vote to the alien, the men who had no interest in the country, who knew nothing about our interests, whose interests and leaning and longings were all for the old land of Germariy or Austria from which they came, the result would have been different. He suggested that if we had allow these three or four hundred thousand aliens to swamp the vote of the Canadians in this country his party would have been *successful, and there would have been no

riot in Quebec. I honestly believe that statement is true, but the people of Canada were not, so inclined, and at the election on the 17th of December they not only gave this Government a mandate to enforce the Military Service Act, to take the necessary number of men for the reinforcements at the front, but they said that this Act which deprived these Germans of the right to vote as British citizens was absolutely to their liking and was good common sense.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext: Members of the Cabinet said quite the contrary, and yet the Cabinet has been sustained. The War-time Elections Act was not the policy of the present Government, it was the policy of the preceding Government; and many of the men who sit in the' Cabinet to-day denounced it, and -quite properly so.

I think, Mr. Speaker,
that one member to-day, the hon. member for North Simcoe has very properly said that the members behind the Government on this occasion are not rubber stamps, that we have minds of our own, and that we say exactly what we think. If I am asked what I think about that particular measure I will say this:	That if the present Government are not in favour of it their judgment is not as good as the judgment of the late Government, because the late Government were absolutely right in passing a measure of that kind. So far as I am personally concerned I believe the verdict of the people on the 17th of December last, means one thing, if no other, namely that the people of Canada gave to this Government, whether they are Unionist or Conservative or whatever they may be, the mandate to support the boys who so sorely need that support to-day. They gave them the right to take, not 100,000 or 200,000, or whatever men were necessary for reinforcements, but they gave their mandate that, so far as humanly possible, every part of Canada should do its share in supplying men. I think it is idle to give excuses. I think the representatives of Quebec would employ their time far better if they would apologize for the occurrences in Quebec, instead of trying to defend them.

Mr. Speaker, your French Canadian colleagues, and especially the residents of the city of Quebec, who are members of this House, have a special interest in the subject-matter of the present debate. 'In both of these capacities, I feel that it is my duty not to remain silent. No doubt we are

passing through a serious stage. Overseas millions of men are engaged in the fight, and we are proud indeed that in this battle for the supremacy of civilization and democracy, we count hundreds of thousands of our compatriots. Two weeks ago the struggle entered upon what many believe to be its final stage. I think, as has been pointed out by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), it is beyond question that very much depends upon the issue, and the hearts of the people of the whole country are lifted up in intercession that the right may prevail. It is therefore deplorable beyond expression that at such a time as this an ugly outbreak and disturbance of the peace should occur, in this country. For us Quebeckers and French Canadians it is sickening end almost unbelievable to think that such shocking incidents should take place' in our dear, old, peaceful city of Quebec. Nobody resents it more than we do. For the outsider the incident will have only ah historic importance. Many will come to Quebec to visit the spot where it occurred, to see the places where the machine guns were laid on the mob and to see the streets where the men fell. But we Quebeckers who live there shall constantly have a remembrance of the disgrace that took place last week.
By what I have been able to gather, from what has been said by hon. members on the other side of the House, the necessity for the drastic enactments contained in the Orders in Council laid on the table of the House was due to the lack of response on the part of the French Canadians to the appeal to them to willingly enlist, either under the system of voluntary recruiting or since the Compulsory Military Service Act was brought into force.
Sir, allow me to take exception to that statement. There is no lack of ideals on the part of the French Canadians. The ideals of the French Canadians are not emotions and passions, as was stated a few moments ago. The patriotism of the French Canadians of the province of Quebec lies in a clear comprehension of the true interests of this country. This clear comprehension, Sir, is not alone the heritage or the property of the French Canadians. The clear comprehension of the interests of every country has been the decisive motive that has led every country and dictated the action of every country in this war. What did the English statesmen consider before they decided to enter the war on the side of France and the other Allies? A few days before the declaration of war the French Ambassador at Petrograd, in consultation with
his Russian colleague, tried to induce the English Ambassador to make a formal declaration that England would be on the side of France and Russia if war broke out. What did Sir Edward Grey instruct his ambassador to respond? He said that England would not side in the war with France and Russia unless British interests required it. That is contained clearly in the diplomatic papers. The French Ambassador urged England to declare that .she would be on the side of France and Russia, and he went so far as to say that if such a declaration were made war would not be declared by Germany. Notwithstanding that, English diplomacy stood by the contention that England would not enter the war unless British interests required it. While Sir Edward Grey was declaring, that unless British interests would lead England into the war
Mr. Speaker,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I was held down pretty closely to the rules and I would suggest to you that the hon. member is travelling pretty far from the question before the House.

I understand the point of the order raised, but I made an assertion, and what I am saying is preliminary to establishing it. I made the assertion that the French Canadians in the province of Quebec comprehended the interests of this, country, and that in looking at the situation, purely from- the point of view of Canadian interests, they are acting in the same way as the British diplomats did. I do not blame England for having considered British interests before committing the country to war. We considered that Canadian interests were at stake and we looked at that directly. A few. months after the declaration of war a message of the President of the United States was issued urging the people of that country to stay neutral because that was in the interest of the United States. Only after three years had passed did the United States enter the war. Did they enter the war when Belgium was invaded, when France was attacked and invaded? No, Sir, during those three years the United States, following the same course, doing business as usual, were trading with Germany and Austria, were supplying the enemies of the Allies with munitions, food and weapons to invade Belgium and France, But one day German submarines came across the

ocean, American ships were sunk and American lives were lost. One day the Lusitania was sunk and hundreds of Americans perished. Then the United States entered the war because American interests were at stake. 'I say, Sir, that true Canadian patriotism must not be carried off its feet simply by the fixed idea that the war can be run only with men, that the war can be won only through the instrumentality of the Military Service Act, and that even if we take another standpoint we are not patriots and true Canadians.
Sir, it has been stated to-day that we did not respond to the Military Service Act, and that has aroused the sentiment of the population of the other provinces against the province of Quebec. We have sent four hundred thousand men overseas, we have spent almost two thousand million dollars, and we now stand alongside the United States, who, for three years, have enriched themselves with the millions derived from trading with Germany, and who during that period did not send a single man overseas. If we are allied in this war we are partners in the same enterprise and to the same end; but in a partnership every partner must do his duty. What would you think of two merchants, partners in a store if one would go in the morning and open the store, sell to customers the whole day long and put money in the cash box when it was empty, and the other would go at nine o'clock, smoke a cigar, simply chat with the customers, take one half of the earnings when he required it, and walk away at night? Such a partnership would not be fair, and would not long continue. Sir, if we are partners in the war the' United States must do their share, and they have the men to enable them to do so. It is useless to contend that Canada must send one hundred thousand men more to win the war; the men are not required. The men are required only for the political , purposes of those who apply the Military Service Act. Why do the Americans refrain from sending men to the front? Their contention is that they have no ships. How is it, then, that after sending overseas four hundred thousand men we have the vessels wherewith to send one hundred thousand more, and yet the Americans have no ships for the transportation of their soldiers?

Where does the hon. gentleman get the information that no American troops have been sent overseas?

Mr. VIEN': I do not say that no American troops have been sent, but I take the declaration of the United States Minister of War for anything I say in this regard. A certain number of American troops have gone overseas, but there are two million men now available in the United States. Why do not the United States send those two million men across the ocean? Because they say, they have no ships with which to transport them.

Is the hon. gentleman
trying to make the argument that Canada should not reinforce her men at the front, but leave them to die like rats in the trenches until such time as two million Americans were sent over? If so what has that got to do with the resolution before the House?

I was coming to that point. I am trying to make that point clear to the minds of my English-speaking friends. I have often discussed the matter with them, and I have met with the same objection that the hon. member for North Simcoe has now raised. I say that the contention of the Government is simply a matter of pride, a matter of fulfilling a promise which was certainly made without due consideration. Why should we keep five divisions, or four divisions, or two divisions at the front? If, Sir, we have sufficient men to maintain two divisions at the front and two divisions in the rear, let us keep two divisions in the rear. Sir, we must not forget-and this is an answer to my hon. friend, the	contradictor,-that France
handed over a portion of its front to England, that England assigned a portion of its front to Canada. Why should not Canada to-day hand over a portion of its front to the United States? We have for three years during the war done our duty. Why should we not now, when we are called upon to make a greater effort, allow our partners in the war to do, not better than we have done, but just as much. Sir, this is the point of view of many French Canadians. They look at the matter from a purely Canadian point of view, because it will not be in the interests of Canada to ruin the human, the vital force of the Dominion, and ruin its credit.
In so far as the. sending of 100,000 men overseas is essential to the winning of the war, if it were so, I would immediately approve of it, hut I say that it is not essential, because if a hundred thousand Canadians were kept here, a hundred thousand Americans could be sent overseas to do their

duty and take their .share, and in that light we view the true interest of the Canadian people. We are not in Canada for one year or for twenty-{five years; we must foresee the after-the-war conditions, and in so doing must 'consider to wlhat extent our effort financially, and in so far as man power is concerned, must go.
'Mr. MORPHY: Will the hon. gentleman allow -me a question? 'There are, I believe 4,000 odd French Canadians fighting bravely at the front. Does the argument of the hon. gentleman mean that no further French Canadians should go to support them, and that we should depend upon Americans to support those brave French Canadians at the front?

That is not at all my argument. I take a much wider, a Canadian, point of view. I am' not making any discrimination or undue distinction between any portion o'f 'the elements of Canada in the Tanks of our troops overseas, and in so far as that is concerned, to answer my hon. friend, I might point out what I heard said in a speech at Niagara. When British-born citizens came to settle in Canada before the war, I learn from reliable sources, there was a certain appellation applied to them.. They were called " English sparrows " in some circles here, because the English sparrow has,, had the bad characteristic of going to its neighbour's nest and eating the eggs. When the war broke out, what occurred? The province of Ontario was glad to rank and to number among her sons 60,000 of these " English sparrows," who were not Canadian-born. We bad no " English sparrows " in the province of Quebec. The men who have been sent overseas from our stock are Canadian-horn citizens.
Mr. LEM1IETJX:	And many more than
four thousand.
The number is 4,826.
No, Sir, I have it from a chaplain who was there from the beginning. There are over twenty thousand French Canadians at the front, and the hon. gentleman knows it.

I want to make this argument to show that the population of the province of Quebec were not carried away by simple emotion and passion. They are directed in their conduct during the war by a true understanding of the real interest of Canada and they are foreseeing post bellum conditions.
I have answered the hon. gentleman who said that we were carried away simply by emotion and passion. Let us come now to the sad events which have occurred in Quebec. A complete statement of the facts is now in the possession of the House, and they have been ably narrated by hon. members who have already spoken. I do not wish to cover the ground again, but I think that too great stress cannot be placed upon the fact that among the population of the province of Quebec the disturbance has received the unreserved condemnation of the great mass of all classes. The churches, the liberal professions, the industrial commercial and labor leaders, and the local press have unanimously joined in reprobating it. To hear me out in that statement, and to leave no doubt whatever in the minds of hon. gentlemen, allow me to invoke the unimpeachable testimony of Major General Lessard himself. On the 3rd April, in his statement to the press, as I read it in the five o'clock edition of the Ottawa Journal, he qualifies the whole incident as "the disgraceful conduct of a small number indeed of irresponsible persons inspired and directed by ontside agents." I have cited his words textually. That fact was absolutely evident to everybody down there. I was in Quebec on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, and although not an eyewitness of everything that oeeured, I have made it a point to collect reliable information right at the scene of the disturbance. On the 2nd of April, the Prime Minister made a statement to this House which appears on page 250 of the unrevised Hansard. I cannot agree with my right hon. friend in so far as his appreciation of the action of the local police is concerned, but in the main his statement is corroborated by the subsequent reports laiid on the Table. Allow me to make a very brief summary of what took place and of what the Prime Minister said.
The incidents commenced on Thursday evening. On that evening some Dominion officers were pursued and sustained some injuries from the handling to which they were subjected, but nothing more of importance-I cite the very words of the Prime Minister-seems to have occurred that evening. On Friday an attack was made on the registry office which was ransacked, but very little loss of important documents occurred. The same evening two newspaper offices were attacked and damaged, but there was no great material loss, and there was no bloodshed. On Saturday evening

there was some disorder, the mob appeared very unruly, and military patrols of the local garrison were ordered out, but still there was no bloodshed. That is all that occurred before the active intervention of the military, according to the Prime Minister's own statement, and as supplemented by the reports published in Hansard. It is greatly to be regretted that the newspapers were at first supplied by the Canadian Press with grossly erroneous and exaggerated reports.
The Canadian Press was most unfortunate indeed in the choice of its local representative; or else if the events were correctly reported, and afterwards viciously exaggerated before they were communicated to the newspapers, that is tantamount to an odious conspiracy, and the public has the right to know what influences were brought to bear on the official of the Canadian press and for what purpose this course was taken.
As soon as the disorder broke out, with an apparently commanded unanimity, the press interpreted it as a general loosening of a previously determined and well-organized opposition on the part of the population of the whole province against the application of the Military Service Act. As if to excite a still greater animosity against Quebec, the first disturbance, which now boils down to a simple row, was greatly exaggerated. Belanger, the Government spotter, was reported dying in a hospital, whereas he had simply been blackeyed and had returned home unmolested during the day. Those who have visited the auditorium since the occurrence know that the fire damaged only a few rooms. The breaking of a few windows in the auditorium annex and the .commencement, of fire, easily extinguished, were reported 'as the complete wrecking of the whole auditorium and its-destruction by fire. What the Prime Minister sums up as a very small loss of important records-Hansard page 250-was reported to be the destruction of all the records absolutely essential to the successful application of the Act in Quebec. Immediately after, again with an apparently commanded unanimity, the press intoned a hymn of hate against the oldest province of the Dominion, against one third of the population of this country. This was the prelude to an equally unanimous appeal to the Government for a sturdy treatment of Quebec, which course the Prime Minister later announced and which we now know has been followed. The conduct of the Canadian Press was in the first place,

extremely dangerous, as likely to inflame against each other, as it did, the already excited minds of English and Frenchspeaking people, and as likely to drive the rioters to further excesses. Secondly, it created in the minds of the people the impression that the population of the city and the province at large were backing the disturbance, whmh, we know, was contrary to the fact. I am pleased to see that as soon as the various newspapers had time to send a special representative to the scene, they immediately .proclaimed that the great mass of the population disapproved the movement. As General Les-sard puts it, the whole affair was the result of the disgraceful conduct of a small number indeed of irresponsible persons, inspired and directed by outside aid. But the harm was done, and a thorough investigation should be made to place the responsibility where it should lie. The press is a power in this country, but the essential condition of the-privileges and liberties which it enjoys is that it should not become mischievous and a danger to public peace. On the other hand, the newspapers which in good faith published reports received from the Canadian press should see that they are not deceived in future, and that the offenders are punished. Before long it is not improbable that we shall know what influence was brought to bear on the official of the Canadian press to cause it to give out isuch grossly exaggerated reports.
Bet us now consider the intervention of the military, and whether it was justified by the facts. All members of the House will agree that in such a riot or outbreak the first consideration of the officers should be that of preventing bloodshed. Bloodshed is the most regrettable incident of the whole affair. On the first evening some Dominion officers suffered injury through the handling to which they were subjected. On the second evening the registry office was ransacked, but little loss of important records occurred. The newspaper offices were wrecked, but there was no bloodshed, and the mayor thought that he could deal with the situation; that military assistance was not required. But by reference to Hansard, page 300, it will be seen that the Government intervened; they sent to Quebec a Toronto regiment, which paraded the streets with .machine guns; and'then the bloodshed took place. Happily the situation is now well under control. To many the action of the Government in causing the military to intervene in the Quebec trouble will appear to be a strong and commend-

able move. I ishall agree with them if such a course was, first, in conformity with the cardinal principles of British Government; second, in conformity with the law of this country; third, justified by the facts; fourth, prudently carried out. We all agree that peace and good order must prevail; their maintenance is the very object of the existence of public institutions. Strong action on the part of the public authority in its proper sphere is desirable. The aid of the military and the civil power in some circumstances is also desirable, and it is especially provided for by the law. But, on the other hand, it has always been a cardinal principle of British government that the military power should be the servant, not the master, of the civil authority. Our compatriots the Orangemen-I shall call them my compatriots, for they are Canadians and so am I-my compatriots, the Orangemen of this country, still gloriously celebrate on the 12th July the Battle of the Boyne. But the Battle of the Boyne was the final incident of a big revolution. The real results ojf the revolution had been previously embodied in 1639 in the Bill of Rights which supplemented the Magna Charta. Among other things laid down in the Bill of Rights was the denial of the two things against which we are now fighting-the Divine right of Kings or Kaiserism-and secondly, militarism. To deny the Divine right of Kings, the Bill of Rights provided that the civil list which up to that time it had been customary to vote for life on the accession of each sovereign would in future be voted yearly. To safeguard against militarism and to prevent the Army from being controlled by the King, the Bill provided that the Army Act should also be voted yearly. King William III, one of the greatest soldiers who ever sat upon the British throne, only came to the throne by solemnly abjuring the exaltation of the military over the civil power. These principles are the rock bottom upon which is based the British Constitution, and they constantly receive the wholehearted support of every true Englishman.	.
These principles have received constant application, in Great Britain, the United States and Canada. The United States went so far as to wage the War of Independence to guard against the enforcement of an obnoxious tax by armed force. In Canada this Parliament has restricted by statute the interference of the military power in civil affairs, even for the maintenance of
peace and good order. Our Militia Act not only specifies the case in which the militia can be called out in aid of the civil power, but carefully prescribes the procedure, which is supplemented by the King's Regulations. It will be illuminating at this moment to read the provisions of the Militia Act, contained in section 80 and the following sections of chapter 41 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
SO. The Active Militia, or any corps thereof, shall be liable to be called out, within or without the municipality in which such corps is raised or organized, for active service, with their arms and ammunition, in aid of the civil power, in any case in which a riot or disturbance of the peace requiring such service occurs, or is, in the opinion of the civil authority hereinafter designated in that behalf, anticipated as likely to occur, and, in either case, beyond the powers of the civil authorities to suppress, or to prevent or deal with.
81. The district officer commanding in any locality, if he is present in the locality and able to act, or if he is not so present, or from sickness or other cause is unable to act, the senior officer of the Active Militia in any locality, not from sickness or other cause unable to act, shall call out the Active Militia, or such portion thereof as he considers necessary for the .purpose of preventing or suppressing any such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance, when thereunto required in writing by the civil authority hereinafter designated in that behalf:	Provided that so far as the
Permanent Force is available, a sufficient number of the Force is to be employed upon the duty of preventing or suppressing such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance before recourse is had to other militia corps, and shall replace such other militia corps if so called out upon duty so soon as and to the extent the Permanent Force shall thereafter become avail-
The Act specifically provides that the active militia shall not be called out on active service unless required, in writing, by the civil authority. We have also the British North America Act, which entrusts the provincial legislatures with the maintenance of peace and good order, with authority to enact police regulations. In this country, as well as in England and the United States, the police organizations are essentially municipal, and everything pertaining to municipal matters comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial authority. (British North America Act, section 92, pp. 8 and 16.) These principles have been upheld time and again by the Privy Council. Thus, in British institutions the military power is made the servant of the civil authority. Our Constitution leaves to the province the maintenance of peace and good order in all municipal affairs. Even in the administration of justice the provincial Attorney General is the proper authority. The Militia Act limits to very specific cases the

intervention of the military power, in aid and upon the request of the civil authorities.
Let us now come back to the complete facts of this case. The disturbance of the peace was local in character. At first there was no bloodshed, but some government policemen were roughly handled, a few windows were broken, some documents der stroyed and building set on fire. The police could not prevent everything, but they did prevent bloodshed. The general officer commanding assures the mayor that military assistance is available, but the mayor declares that he can deal with the situation, that military assistance is not required, and that he is aJble to cope alone with any outbreak. This is contained in the statement laid on the Table by the Prime Minister himself, and reported on page 300 of Hansard. In such a case was- the Government justified in calling on the military to intervene? No, Sir. The cardinal principles of British government, the constitutional laws of this country, the special Act provided to govern the militia, condemn the Government -and the military authorities. Until then no bloodshed had taken place. It was only when the Government had chosen to reinforce the -garrison at Quebec, and bring into action all the military machinery, that blood was shed. Was that course justified? The Prime Minister himself has taken the trouble to give evidence to the country. (Hansard, page 250.) An adequate effort by -the local authority would have put down the disturbance. Then, surely in the case of failure by the municipal authorities, an appeal from them to the local garrison would have been amply sufficient.
The mayor was in conference with the general officer commanding and was supplied by him with a copy of the Riot Act. He proceeded to the place of the disturbance and succeeded in reducing the effect of the disturbance, the result being that while some windows were smashed, there was very little loss of property. Without authority and without necessity, the federal authority inflamed the smouldering embers by bringing to Quebec a Toronto regiment. Other cities in the past have been the theatre of such deplorable incidents, but the military authorities never intervened before being called upon to lend assistance to the civil powers, as provided by law. What would the good people of Toronto say if,.in order to quell a disturbance in that city, a Quebec regiment were sent there with machine guns. They would pelt with rocks and stones the damned Frenchmen from Quebec. Excuse 
the expression, but I want to be accurate -they would shoot at them with firearms of various kinds. This is what was done in Quebec. (See Prime Minister's speech, Hansard page 251). The facts narrated by the Prime Minister would never justify such an outrageous intervention by the militia. This was a gross and most imprudent transgression of the law. This incident exemplifies the soundness of the principles laid down by the right hon. leader of the Opposition; that is to say, the desirability of at all times following the law. I said, Sir, that, as a consequence of this transgression, and of the outrage to the people ofi Quebec by calling Toronto regiments to Quebec to march through their streets with machine guns, the excitement of the mob naturally greatly increased, and then only did bloodshed ocur. The Prime Minister has endeavoured to shirk responsibility from his shoulders, and to very generously shift it to the municipal authorities of Quebec, stating, and I might be allowed to use this note to quote, textually, the words of the Prime Minister, so that my hon. friend might not take exception to it. The disturbance might have been put down without much difficulty, if proper effort had been made by civic authorities.
The Prime Minister, to my mind, only succeeded in clearly establishing that the affair was a purely local one, such as occasionally occurs in every city, and nothing warranted the nation-wide importance which was given to it by the press and by the Government. The Government which so forcibly declared its intention to see that the law is strictly adhered to gave us a very poor example of obedience to the law. As wrong is ordinarily followed by wrong, and as one illegality leads to another, the military intervention has caused serious bloodshed, the responsibility for which lies exclusively with the Government. The Prime Minister's insinuation that the local authorities were not disposed to observe public order is not worthy of his high office. (Page 251 of Hansard). No statement is less warranted by the facts. In the state of excitement of the mob, the police did very well, indeed, to prevent bloodshed and limit the effect of the disturbance to rough handling of some undiscriminating Government spotters. The breaking of a few windows and a little loss of important records were all that occurred. The disorder, Sir, would surely have died away with no other consequences, had not the Government been guilty of a very unwise, ill-timed, unlawful and outrageous intervention. During this occurrence, the local authorities showed great wisdom and consideration, and knowledge of the character of the population. The Government, if not actuated by political motives, have not shown justifiable grounds for their action and their intervention. The Orders in Council which have been laid on the Table of the House involve a serious departure from the ordinary course of constitutional law in England. Disturbances more serious than the riots at Quebec have occurred in England and Ireland and the Government of England did not see fit to suspend the constitution of the country. Might I cite one instance in which the Government of Great Britain might have been justified in taking drastic steps?. Will my friends the Orangemen of this country kindly remember what occurred when King Carson organized an army of 60,000 men to resist the application of Home Rule? He armed these men with the outspoken intention of resisting the application of the law. Did the British Government suspend the constitution? Did the British Government recall the Magna Charta or the Bill of Rights? No such thing was done. British institutions were strictly adhered to. What did England itself do in Ireland during this war? A Military Service Act was enacted in England. Was it applied to Ireland? No. Why? Because the Irish people did not want it.
What have we to do with Ireland? The hon. gentleman has travelled all over the world.

I am citing these instances
to show that the Government, on the present occasion, put aside the constitution of the country, that they were not justified by the circumstances and that they will find no precedent to sustain their conduct in this- regard. They will not find any precedent in England, in 'Ireland, in Australia, in America or any place in the world.
Except Germany.

Except Germany, and I was coming to that. We are fighting against Kaiserism, against bossism, against Prus-sianism. What are these appellations? What do they mean? They mean the encroachment of an organized military Government against the freedom of modern democracy. If we want to make the world free for democracy, which is stated to be the intention of the allied countries, we must not follow the same path that the Kaiser has followed on the other side. We must not introduce into this country Prus-sianism and Kaiserism with their results.
Canadian' blood has been shed in Quebec. A few years ago a great strike broke out in France. The employees of the various public utilities quit work. The telegraphers and

Parliament and to shoiw 'to the whole world that his hands were clean of French 'blood. I think that if a better un-derfMr. Vien.l
standing of t'he French Canadian point of view were arrived at by the English-speaking side of the House no such thing would be possible. I think that through a more intimate intercourse we could come to understand each other's point of view more intelligently and more closely. We do not criticize the English-speaking element of Canada, neither do we want to impo&e our views on them. We do not wish to enact laws to govern them, our desire is that they shall be free to do as they please under the British flag. But, at the same time, Sir, we ol-aim the same privileges for ourselves. If this is a free country, and we are to continue to enjoy the liberty to which we are entitled, all will be well. But I say that the provisions contained in the Order in Council laid on the Table to-day are opposed to that liberty, and if they are put into force I am afraid this beautiful Canada of ours will not be a happy country to live in. I am afraid that grave danger of disruption is impending, and that the Government is not taking the necessary steps to eliminate that danger in the future. As I have already said, we are law-abiding citizens, and we will continue to he so, but there is not the slightest reason why a vicious reflection should be made on the character of a whole population because of the occurrence of a riot of a merely local character.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I would be doing very much less than my duty to my constituents who elected me to Parliament on the 17th of December last, to say nothing of ignoring my own very strong feelings on the subject, were I to remain silent and not to express my views on the subject under discussion. I come not from Ontario, nor from any part of Quebec, where possibly historic conditions may be responsible for local feeling or prejudices, but from western Canada, where I can assure you there is no feeling or prejudice against any nationality or any special race. I,n the West we regard ourselves as Canadians and we think that answers all requirements. For us there are no especially favoured communities ; and we feel that as Canadians, as members of a free community of the British Empire we have very great rights and privileges, and that it is our duty now, and whenever occasion may demand, to fight as fuliy as may be in our power for those rights and privileges. I do ncvt think I am taking an unreasonable view in expressing the belief that the willingness to fight for the rights and privileges we enjoy should be coexistent with their enjoyment. I am absolutely free, as I

believe the people generally in our province are absolutely free, from any prejudice. But we do feel, for two reasons- first, (that we need the men, and secondly, because the province from which I come, and perhaps other parts of Canada have done more towards sending men overseas than have been done in the province of Quebec- that more men should be sent to the firing line from that province. The mandate which was given to me, equally, I believe, with the mandate which was given to other members who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, on the 17th of December last, was that we should come to Ottawa and do our utmost to enforce the Military Service Act, not only in a similar manner in each province, but also that like results should be obtained from one end of Canada to the other. That, I feel, is the reason that I was sent here by my constituents, and, to be frank, I have grave doubts as to whether I was sent here for any other reason. Such being the case and such being my own personal belief and feeling, I intend to do what little I can here to see that the Act in question is carried out absolutely and entirely.
As regards the riots that have taken place in Quebec, I do not think the Government have gone too far in'the way in which they have attempted, and have to some extent succeeded in enforcing this Act in that province. The previous enlistments in the province of Quebec for service overseas were not nearly as great as in other parts of Canada, and while, under the Military Service Act, one hundred and seventeen thousand, men have registered-there are still a great many who have not done so-the province of Quebec has sent overseas only some three thousand, or less. Under the circumstances it seems to me that we have a right to demand that more men shall be obtained from that province. I believe that the enforcement of the Military Service Act up to date in the province of Quebec has not been successful. Therefore, it is necessary for such changes to be made in the Act as will ensure a greater degree of success. I wish to congratulate the Government on the Orders in Council deailing with this subject which they have brought down. I believe that each and every one of them will make the Military Service Act more successful, and our opinion is that the changes necessary to render the Act more successful must be made.
I feel that if it is not made successful, and that if we do not obtain, and obtain speedily, from the province of Quebec as many soldiers to go overseas as the rest
of Canada has furnished, each and every one of us who have come here with very, very clear orders given on the 17th day of December, will have failed to do our duty in carrying out our instructions, and that we are not worthy to represent the people who have sent us here.
I have listened to-day to various speeches by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side, in which they have professed a willingness to obey the law, and to participate, as far as Canada is concerned, fairly and equally in this war. I am not going to say what may be the actual beliefs or feelings of those hon. gentlemen, but it does occur to me, afteT listening to their speeches, that the result of their words cannot in any sense be calculated to cause those who follow them to be more anxious or more likely to obey the law; nor do I think that the consequence or effect of their words will in any way increase recruiting. By the plainest of logic, and the use of the most ordinary commonsense, one cannot come to the conclusion that these hon. gentlemen are very anxious to assist recruiting or exceedingly anxious that the law should be obeyed. I would not care to be in the position of those hon. gentlemen, who can exercise influence over their people to the proper end, and who have influenced them in the manner which they have taken here to-day. Various arguments have been put up, the usual arguments we have heard before, that these men should be retained at home for food production. Food production and other industries are all very fine. But men are needed at the front, and when men go overseas, very often they get killed, and each part of Canada should bear its share of that risk. I know of no reason why that should not be.
I would remind hon. gentlemen that they are here to-day enjoying the rights and privileges of British citizenship, and while they are right in protecting those rights and privileges, if we do not send men overseas, and if we do not do our part, and others do not do theirs, we shall see such a sweeping away of British rights and privileges that there will be none left. I have seen the work of the Germans. I have been overseas and have seen them doing their work. And we on this side are doing what should be done in this country to preserve these various rights and privileges, about which we have heard so much talk.

In closing, I wish to answer the remark made by my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), who asserted that Le Devoir had published seditious1 articles, and that Henri Bourassa ought to he interned.
